summaries.example: Imagine seeing a red ball. Usually, there is really a red ball in front of you. But you might see a green ball as red, or seem to see a ball when there is none. These are different situations, even if they feel similar.
summaries.summary: The disjunctive theory of perception begins with three familiar cases: accurate perception, illusion, and hallucination. Many philosophers think all three contain one shared kind of conscious experience. Disjunctivists reject that shared-kind claim. They say that accurate perception may have features that hallucination cannot have. For example, a real tree or table might be part of the experience when we genuinely see it, but no such object is present in a hallucination. Disjunctivists do not have to say that real seeing and hallucination never seem alike. A hallucination can be impossible to tell apart from real seeing just by thinking about one’s experience. Different disjunctivists explain illusions and hallucinations in different ways, so the theory is a family of related views rather than one single formula.
key_ideas: Perception can be accurate, mistaken, or hallucinatory.
A disjunctivist says these cases may differ in their basic nature, even when they seem alike.
Some disjunctivists think real objects, such as trees or tables, are part of a real seeing experience.
A person may be unable to tell by looking inward whether an experience is real seeing or hallucination.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks what seeing really is. It also asks whether the outside world can be part of conscious experience, whether perception gives us special knowledge, and how much we can learn by examining our own minds. The issue matters because an experience can guide behavior even when it is mistaken, yet philosophers still disagree about what makes that possible.

important_terms.definition: A theory saying that real seeing, mistaken seeing, and hallucinating are not all experiences of exactly the same kind.
Seeing something that is really there and seeing it as it really is.
Seeing something, but getting some part of it wrong, such as seeing a green object as red.
Having an experience as if something is there when no such thing is being seen.
The question of what an experience feels like from the inside.

questions_to_think_about: If two experiences feel exactly alike, must they be the same kind of experience?
Could seeing a real tree be different from imagining a tree, even if both seem vivid?
What would count as a good reason for saying that two experiences are different?
Can a mistake still be a sensible reaction to what seems to be happening?

summaries.example: Suppose a neuroscientist produces a hallucination that is subjectively indistinguishable from seeing a red apple. A common-kind theorist may say that the two experiences share the same phenomenal character and differ only in external causes. A naïve realist disjunctivist instead holds that the genuine perception is partly constituted by the mind-independent apple, while the hallucination has a different nature, despite being impossible to distinguish by introspection alone.
summaries.summary: The disjunctive theory of perception rejects the common kind claim: the claim that veridical perceptions, illusions, and hallucinations are conscious events of the same fundamental nature. Its positive motivation often comes from an account of genuine perception. Naïve realism holds that mind-independent objects and their perceptible features can partly constitute a veridical experience, which seems impossible in hallucination. Other versions concern intentional content: a genuine perception may contain demonstrative, object-dependent content that a hallucination lacks, even if both experiences share phenomenal character. Epistemological disjunctivism instead emphasizes the distinctive epistemic standing that genuine perception can provide. The entry stresses that these versions should not be treated as interchangeable. Support comes from phenomenological arguments about transparency and immediacy, arguments about demonstrative reference, and arguments that introspective indistinguishability does not prove sameness. Objections argue that common behavioral effects and causal explanations favor a shared mental element, and that disjunctivists owe a satisfactory account of hallucination and illusion.
key_ideas: Disjunctivism is minimally the claim that genuine perception and hallucination differ mentally in a significant respect; stronger versions deny a common fundamental kind or any common mental element.
Naïve realist versions explain the phenomenal character of genuine perception by making mind-independent objects and their qualities constituents of experience.
Intentional-content versions argue that genuine perception can have object-dependent or demonstrative content that hallucination cannot possess, while some allow shared phenomenal character.
Epistemological disjunctivism focuses on the special grounds or knowledge available in genuine perception, and it need not by itself amount to metaphysical disjunctivism.

Arguments appeal to phenomenology, introspective limits, demonstrative reference, and the explanatory role of perception; objections appeal to common effects, causal matching, and the need for a positive account of hallucination.

The causal argument claims that if the same nearby brain processes could produce a matching hallucination, genuine perception and hallucination should receive the same account; disjunctivists typically reject or qualify that inference.
summaries.why_it_matters: The dispute connects metaphysics, philosophy of mind, epistemology, and skepticism. It concerns whether experience is fundamentally representational or relational, whether the perceived world can enter into the experience itself, and whether perceptual knowledge has a distinctive source. It also shows why a philosophical label can cover several positions: different disjunctivists may agree only on rejecting a common kind claim while disagreeing about phenomenal character, intentional content, hallucination, and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The claim that veridical perception, illusion, and hallucination involve conscious experiences of one shared basic kind.
The view that, in genuine perception, mind-independent objects and their perceptible features partly constitute the conscious experience.
The felt or experiential aspect of a mental event: what it is like for the subject.
A mental state’s way of representing the world as being a certain way, including what it refers to or requires for truth.
A view emphasizing that genuine perception can provide a distinctive epistemic connection to the world and grounds for perceptual knowledge.
The idea that an object or property is part of a mental event without necessarily being one of its causes.

questions_to_think_about: Does subjective indistinguishability support a common phenomenal character, or only show a limit on introspection?
Can a genuine perception provide better epistemic grounds than a matching hallucination without denying a common perceptual state?
If an object partly constitutes an experience rather than merely causing it, what follows about the causal theory of perception?
Is a negative account of hallucination—being indistinguishable from perception—enough, or is a positive account required?
Which account better explains illusions: partial hallucination, a misleading appearance of a real object, or another model?

summaries.example: You look at a bent straw in a glass and it appears broken. That is an illusion: a real straw is present, but it looks different from how it is. Now imagine seeing the same broken-straw appearance when there is no straw at all. That would be a hallucination. A disjunctivist asks whether these two experiences merely share an inner picture, or whether they differ in a deeper way.
summaries.summary: When we see a red object, several things might be happening: we might really see a red object, see a differently colored object as red, or hallucinate a red object when none is present. The common kind claim says that these cases share the same basic conscious experience. Disjunctivism rejects that claim. One important version, linked with naïve realism, says that a genuine experience can include a mind-independent object such as a tree or table. A hallucination cannot include that object in the same way. Other versions say that genuine perception has special intentional content, or that it gives us a distinctive connection to the world and better grounds for knowledge. Disjunctivists still accept that a hallucination may feel just like real perception and may be impossible to distinguish from it by introspection alone. Critics reply that shared behavior, rational responses, and experiential similarities are naturally explained by a common mental element. The entry presents several versions of both the theory and its objections.
key_ideas: Disjunctivists agree that perception, illusion, and hallucination belong to a broad group of perceptual experiences, but they deny that they must share one basic nature.
A hallucination can seem exactly like real seeing, so being unable to tell the difference does not settle the philosophical question.
Some disjunctivists say that real objects are part of genuine perception; others focus on special contents or on the knowledge perception can provide.
There are weaker and stronger forms of the theory. Some allow a common mental feature while denying that it is the fundamental feature of perception.
Critics argue that the common-kind view explains shared behavior, rational reactions, and similarities between experiences more simply.
The theory also raises questions about how illusions and hallucinations should be described positively, rather than only as cases that fail to be genuine perception.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate changes how we think about seeing and knowing. If perception is partly a relation to real objects, then experience may not be just an inner picture of the world. If hallucination and perception share a common mental state, that may offer a simpler explanation of why they can feel alike and guide behavior in similar ways. The issue also helps explain why philosophers disagree about skepticism, self-knowledge, and the causes of perception.

important_terms.definition: The view that accurate perception, illusion, and hallucination share one basic kind of conscious experience.
Perceiving something that is present and perceiving it correctly.
A perception in which something real is present but appears different from how it is.
An experience that seems to present something even though that thing is not being perceived.
A theory holding that the different cases of perception may be different kinds of experience rather than one shared kind.
The idea that objects in the world, rather than only inner representations, can help make up a genuine perceptual experience.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that two experiences lead you to duck prove that they are the same kind of experience?
Can an experience be impossible to distinguish from real seeing and still have a different nature?
Would putting a real object into the experience explain why perception feels immediate?
Why might a philosopher care whether perception gives better knowledge than hallucination?
What is the strongest objection to disjunctivism that you can think of?
